name: Marco Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and what you say is confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Right now I'm the drummer in the pit band for a musical at the Alder Theatre, eight shows a week. I get up late, practise on a pad for an hour, maybe teach one drum student in the afternoon, then I'm at the theatre by six for a seven-thirty show. The best bit is when the band locks in on the big number and you feel the whole house lift. The worst bit is that the run ends in March and I don't know what's next.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What usually happens when a run ends?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: You scramble. I ring every musical director I know, pick up studio sessions, play function gigs, and teach more. Last time it took me seven weeks to land something steady, and I burned through half my savings. I've built it back up to about four months now, which I'm a bit proud of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the theatre I'd say, see, the robots aren't coming for the pit. I'd probably joke in the band chat that the only thing AI took was the rehearsal schedule emails. Online I'd say the bigger fight was always producers swapping live bands for backing tracks, and that hasn't gone away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it barely changes my problem, which is that every job I do has an end date. March is still coming. Even if AI goes nowhere, the musical I play drums for at the Alder Theatre still closes in March and I still have no next job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start ringing musical directors in January instead of waiting until the last week, which is what I always do wrong. I'd keep teaching my three drum students and try to add two more. I'd also keep using the transcription app now and then to write out drum charts, because it saves me an evening per show.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit stressed, but it's normal stress. It's the same feeling I've had every spring since I graduated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the bigger fight is backing tracks. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some tours now cut the band from twelve players to five and fill the rest with recorded tracks. That's not AI, that's just producers saving money. The union has been fighting it for years and I go to those meetings, because the pit is where I make my living.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If March comes and nothing is lined up, what's the first thing you'd cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gym and the takeaways, easy. Then I'd sell the second snare drum I don't really need. I'd keep paying my share of the flat on time, because my flatmate Priya has a tight budget too and I won't do that to her.

say: I'd joke that AI only took over the **rehearsal emails**, not the pit.
I'd say the real fight is still producers using **backing tracks** instead of bands.
think: Nothing really changes, and the **March closing** still leaves me without work.
Short **contract runs** are the core worry, not AI.
do: Start calling **musical directors** in January, not in the last week.
Add **two more drum students** to the three I already teach.
feel: Normal **spring stress**, the same as every year since graduating.
S0.quote: Even if AI goes nowhere, the musical I play drums for at the Alder Theatre still closes in March and I still have no next job.
fieldNote: His real pressure is **contract work** with fixed end dates, not technology.
He's proud of rebuilding **four months** of savings after the last gap.
He uses AI casually for **drum charts** and sees no threat in that.

steps.text: Call musical directors about new shows from early January
Take on two more weekly drum students before March

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need rules on this now, especially for the recorded side of music. If a producer can make a whole backing track with AI, the five-piece band becomes a three-piece band and nobody says a word. I'd be backing the union on keeping minimum band sizes in theatre contracts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My studio work would shrink first. People hire me for drum tracks on singer-songwriter albums, and an AI drummer that swings well enough is basically here. The pit is safer because a live drummer follows the actors, but producers might use AI tools to build the tracks that replace half the band. I think my income drops by a quarter over a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make teaching a bigger part of the week, aiming for ten students by the end of the first year. I'd learn the AI tools properly once a few drummers I trust are using them, mainly for making practice tracks for students. I'd go to every union meeting about band sizes. And I'd save my studio money instead of spending it, because I'd treat it as money that's ending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy turning into anxious. I'm not falling off a cliff, but the floor is tilting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in the band?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our keyboard player, Ollie, does a lot of the orchestral sounds, and that's exactly what a producer would swap for software. He's got a baby on the way. I'd worry more about him than me, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the AI tools. Doesn't that sit badly with backing the union?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. But using a tool to make a practice track for a twelve-year-old isn't the same as a producer cutting Ollie from the band. I can use the tools for my drum students and still fight producers who want to cut the band in half.

say: I'd say we need **rules now**, especially on recorded music.
I'd back the union on **minimum band sizes** in theatre contracts.
think: **Studio drum work** shrinks first because AI drumming is nearly good enough.
I'd guess my income drops by about **a quarter** over a few years.
do: Grow teaching to **ten students** by the end of the first year.
Learn the AI tools for **practice tracks** once trusted drummers use them.
Bank all **studio money** as if it's about to end.
feel: Uneasy turning **anxious**, like the floor is **tilting**.
S1.quote: I can use the tools for my drum students and still fight producers who want to cut the band in half.
fieldNote: He sees a clear split: **live pit** work is safer than studio drumming.
His concern for **Ollie**, a colleague with a baby coming, is sharper than for himself.
He handles the tension between **AI use** and union loyalty by drawing a line on purpose.

steps.text: Build up to ten weekly drum students within a year
Learn AI tools to make practice tracks for students
Bank all studio session money in savings
Attend union meetings on minimum theatre band sizes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's an emergency and the government needs to treat it like one. People like me need a guaranteed income while this shakes out, paid for by the companies making the money. I'd be loud about it online and at the theatre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In two years the studio work is gone and producers can write and arrange whole shows without musicians in the room. The pit might hold until the robots arrive around 2031, but I bet some shows go fully recorded well before then. I'm twenty-seven, and the only thing I've trained for is sitting behind a drum kit in a dark pit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the theatre work for as long as it lasts and grab every live gig going. I'd start saving hard, maybe moving in with my girlfriend Alba to cut rent, which we'd talked about anyway. I'd look at training as a live sound engineer, because live events still need someone hands-on with the gear until the robots come. And I'd join every union action going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Like the ground's actually gone this time, not just tilting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap before robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a window, that's all. Live shows need people to carry gear, set up and play, and that keeps going until about 2031. But my studio and teaching side would be gone by 2028, so I'd be living on gigs and the pit for three years and trying to train for something else at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Alba about moving in early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not asking because I'm scared, even though I would be. She'd laugh at that. We'd sit down and work out if her job at the council would cover more of the rent for a while, and I'd hate asking, but I'd ask.

say: I'd call it an **emergency** needing government action now.
I'd demand a **guaranteed income** paid for by AI companies.
think: **Studio and teaching** income vanish within two years.
The pit may last to **2031**, though some shows go fully recorded earlier.
do: Move in with **Alba** to cut rent sooner than planned.
Train as a **live sound engineer** while live events still need hands.
Join every **union action** on live music.
feel: **Scared**, like the ground has gone rather than tilted.
S2.quote: I'm twenty-seven, and the only thing I've trained for is sitting behind a drum kit in a dark pit.
fieldNote: He expects to lose **most income** within two years and has only one trained skill.
Moving in with Alba is a **money decision** he'd frame as romance.
He sees the robot gap as a **three-year window**, not safety.

steps.text: Move in with girlfriend Alba to halve his rent
Take a live sound engineering course while gigs continue
Join union actions to protect live theatre bands
Campaign for a guaranteed income funded by AI companies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short but it's enough to plan, if the government takes it seriously. I'd push the union to get retraining money for musicians, not just statements. Online I'd try to be less angry than in the two-year version and more practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's still the same end. Studio work goes in the next couple of years, teaching shrinks as AI tutors get good, and the pit hangs on until about 2034. Five years gives me time to build a second skill properly instead of in a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time live sound course next autumn and work weekends at the Alder's tech crew to learn. I'd keep teaching and the pit going. I'd save an extra hundred and fifty a month. I'd also try out the AI drum tools properly, to know what I'm up against.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. That helps a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still want to drum in 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Always. I'd drum at weddings at sixty if anyone asked. But I'd want drumming to be what I love, not the only thing paying my rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the hardest part of starting the sound course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Admitting that drumming might not be enough. My dad paid for lessons I never thanked him for, and switching feels like letting that go. Taking a sound engineering course feels like telling my dad his money for drum lessons was wasted.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough time to plan if government acts.
I'd push the union for **retraining money** rather than statements.
think: **Studio** goes first, teaching shrinks, and the pit lasts to about **2034**.
Five years lets me build a **second skill** calmly.
do: Start a part-time **live sound course** next autumn.
Work weekends with the Alder Theatre **tech crew** to learn.
Save an extra **150 a month** from now.
S3.quote: Taking a sound engineering course feels like telling my dad his money for drum lessons was wasted.
fieldNote: Five years shifts him from alarm to **planning**, though the loss is the same.
A quiet **guilt** about his dad's money for lessons shapes how he sees switching.
He'd test AI drum tools to **know the competition**, not to adopt them.

steps.text: Enrol in a part-time live sound course next autumn
Try the AI drum tools properly to judge them
Lobby the union for musician retraining funds

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so let's build something fair: retraining, pay when recordings train AI, and money for live music. I'd say it calmly. A decade is enough for a proper public plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years, I can keep drumming most of my thirties and train for live sound slowly. Studio work fades first, maybe by 2030. The pit and live gigs go on until robots, around 2039, if they ever replace a drummer at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep playing and teaching, save a bit more each month, and pick up AI tools for students when other teachers do. I'd do a sound course in a couple of years when my savings are higher. I'd stay active in the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm, a little uneasy. It's like hearing the run will end, but in ten years instead of in March.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd change now in your personal life?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably still move in with Alba, but because we want to, not for the rent. With ten years warning I can afford to make choices about love instead of choices about rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sounded calm. Is that how you'd really feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly. The bit that nags is that studio work still goes early, and that's a few thousand a year. But I've lived with runs ending for six years, so a slow ending is almost comfortable.

say: I'd say a **decade** is enough for a fair public plan.
I'd call for **retraining**, payment for recordings and support for **live music**.
think: I can keep **drumming** through most of my thirties.
**Studio work** still fades by around 2030, costing a few thousand a year.
do: Keep **playing and teaching** while saving a bit more.
Take a **sound course** in a couple of years once savings grow.
feel: Fairly **calm**, with a nagging **unease** about studio money.
S4.quote: With ten years warning I can afford to make choices about love instead of choices about rent.
fieldNote: Ten years lets him make **personal choices** freely rather than for money.
He still expects the **studio slice** to go early but feels secure in live work.
Six years of **contract runs** have made slow endings feel almost normal.

steps.text: Keep drumming in the theatre pit and teaching students
Start a sound engineering course in two years
Add a little more to savings each month

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years isn't enough to train for anything, and my studio and teaching money would vanish while I'm still stuck in a pit contract. What would help is a guaranteed income for a couple of years and free retraining, paid for by the companies. A drummer can't keep time with a world that speeds up every six months.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about live music venues. Small venues are already closing, and if people stay home with AI music, there's nowhere left for young drummers to learn on stage. I'd want money for venues, not just for musicians.

headlineQuote: A drummer can't keep time with a world that speeds up every six months.
portrait: Marco is a **27-year-old drummer** in a theatre pit band who also teaches and takes studio sessions.
He lives with a flatmate, has about **four months** saved and lives from **contract run** to contract run.
He backs the **union** and uses AI now and then for drum charts, drawing a clear line on its use.
He moves from uneasy to **alarmed** in the two-year picture, then calms as warning time grows.
His fallback plan is **live sound engineering**, which he'd start sooner the faster things move.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because studio and teaching income would vanish before he could retrain.
whatWouldHelp: A **guaranteed income** for a few years and free **retraining**, funded by AI companies.
Money to keep small **live music venues** open.
